text: A revenue problem is just a constraint you haven't named yet.

The most expensive number in a business is the one nobody's measuring.

Usually it's the conversion between two stages everyone assumes are fine.

Most owners think it's a lead problem.
Usually it's a follow-up problem.

The symptom is where it hurts. The constraint is where you fix it.

Growth has an order of operations:

1. Find the one constraint limiting everything else
2. Fix it until it's no longer the limit
3. Re-diagnose, the constraint has moved

Most businesses skip step 1 and wonder why effort doesn't turn into growth.

Every company has one constraint that limits everything else.

Right now it's usually one of:
• Retention
• Cash flow
• Sales conversion
• Delivery capacity

Find that one first. Everything downstream gets easier.

Revenue problems are usually symptoms.
Constraints are the disease.

Fastest way to waste a budget:

Scale before you diagnose.

Pricing is the fastest lever you have.

No new leads. No new headcount.
A 10% price increase drops almost straight to margin.

Most businesses are underpriced, because they never actually tested it.

text:
You can learn more in five customer conversations than in five months of analytics.

What to actually ask
parts:
You can learn more in five customer conversations than in five months of analytics.

What to actually ask
One. What were you doing about this before you found us? Tells you who you’re really competing with, which is usually a spreadsheet or nothing.
Two. What nearly stopped you buying? This is the objection your page should be answering and probably isn’t.
Three. How would you describe us to someone like you? Their words are better than your positioning. Use them verbatim.

Don’t defend anything. Don’t explain. Just write down what they say, in their language, and read it back a week later.

Half of what you find will be free money.

text: If you’re building something and nobody’s engaging yet, read this before you quit posting
parts: If you’re building something and nobody’s engaging yet, read this before you quit posting
Reach early is brutal. Most posts from a small account are seen by a couple of dozen people, and that has almost nothing to do with whether the post was good.

Which means judging your idea by early numbers is judging it on the wrong evidence. The signal at that stage is replies, not likes. One person saying "this is exactly my situation" is worth four hundred impressions.
So write for the one person, not the feed. Say the specific thing. The generic version reaches the same nobody and teaches you nothing.

And go and be useful in other people’s replies. That’s the actual distribution channel early on, and it works while your own posts are still finding their footing.

What are you building? Say it below.

text:
Your spreadsheet already knows what is wrong.

Most owners never learn to read it.

Four questions that pull the answer out
parts:
Your spreadsheet already knows what is wrong.

Most owners never learn to read it.

Four questions that pull the answer out
One. Where do people go quiet? Put a percentage between every stage. The lowest one is not a mystery, it is an address.
Two. What does the average hide? Split by source, by segment, by month. Blended numbers are where constraints go to be invisible.
Three. What is this costing? Multiply the gap by the value of a customer. A percentage is an opinion. A dollar figure is a decision.

Four. Did it move? Write the number before you change anything, then check it in thirty days. Without that step you are collecting stories, not evidence.

Save this. Follow for the rest of the system.

text:
Nobody is accountable to a twelve-slide report.

What a useful review looks like
parts:
Nobody is accountable to a twelve-slide report.

What a useful review looks like

One page. What we said was limiting us. What we changed. What moved. What’s limiting us now.

That’s it. Four lines.
The second line is where most reviews quietly fail. "What we changed" has to be specific enough that somebody could disagree with it.
The third is the one people skip. If you never check whether it moved, you’re collecting stories, not evidence, and you’ll try the same fix again next year.

Length is how teams hide from line three.

If the review doesn’t fit on a page, it isn’t a review, it’s a performance.

text:
You were busy all week and the business didn’t move.

Here’s what usually happened
parts:
You were busy all week and the business didn’t move.

Here’s what usually happened
You did ten things at ten percent effort. All ten are now slightly better and none of them crossed the line where anyone outside would notice.
Improvements aren’t linear. Most have a threshold, and under it you get nothing at all. Half a rewrite of a sales page performs exactly like no rewrite.
So the choice isn’t how hard you work. It’s how few things you’re willing to let be bad this week.

Pick one. Take it past the threshold. Let the other nine sit.

Next week they’re still there, and you’ll have one thing that actually landed.

text: If you are building solo and this week felt flat, this thread is for you rather than at you 👇
parts: If you are building solo and this week felt flat, this thread is for you rather than at you 👇
Watching someone with a worse product get all the attention. That is most weeks. The posts you see from people further along skip straight past it, which is why yours feels abnormal when it is not.
What actually helps: make the week smaller. One number, one thing that moves it, and a note of what you expected to happen before you find out.
Writing the expectation down first is the whole trick. Otherwise you will remember having predicted whatever happened, and you will learn nothing from a month of work.

Who is the one person whose reply would make your week?

I read every reply. That is not a growth tactic, I am just also doing this alone.
